items.title: [justinangel.net] Windows Phone 7 – Emulator Automation
items.content_html:
Hi Folks,

In this next blog post we’ll review how to automate the Windows Phone 7 Emulator and what are some real-world usages this technique.

This blog post is the second blog post in a series of unrelated advanced Windows Phone 7 blog posts.
The previous blog post in this series is “Windows Phone 7 – Unlocked ROMs”.

 

Why is Windows Phone 7 Automation Important?

Currently, the Windows Phone 7 Emulator can only launch developer packages (XAPs) from inside Visual Studio 2010.
Meaning, if we’ve got a XAP we can’t get the emulator to load it without Visual Studio.

As we’ve seen in a previous blog post the emulator can be launched and even installed on machines that do not have Visual Studio. More on that here.
Let’s consider that in order to load XAPs into the Emulator we currently have to use Visual Studio. 

The problem is – How do we load XAPs into WP7 Emulators and Devices without using Visual Studio?

So how does our Build Server run nightly tests? Or how do our customers see our applications?

Customers and Build servers don't have Visual Studio 2010 installed.

So, how can we deploy XAPs to an emulator running on these machines?

 

Quit your Jibber-Jabber, show me how to automate the WP7 emulator!

Let’s create a new solution with a Console Application and a Windows Phone 7 Project.

We’ll use the ConsoleApplication as our automation harness that can run on any computer with the .Net framework.
The WindowsPhone Application is the application whose deployment we’ll automate.

 

The CoreCon 10 WP7 API

The secret sauce for WP7 Automation is the CoreCon API.
These CoreCon DLLs have been in deep hibernation since 2007 when they last got a major upgrade.
For WP7 Tools the CoreCon API has been updated and are used by Visual Studio 2010 when deploying applications to WP7 devices and emulators.

Let’s add a reference to Microsoft.SmartDevice.Connectivity.dll from the CoreCon API.
On a x64 developer box, the DLL can be found at: C:\Program Files (x86)\Common Files\microsoft shared\Phone Tools\CoreCon\10.0\Bin\Microsoft.Smartdevice.Connectivity.dll 

 

 

Now that we have the CoreCon DLL reference in place, we can start automating WP7.

Here’s the User Experience we’re aiming for in this demo:

We’ll have to build the following workflow:

     

We’ll start off by getting an instance of the WP7 CoreCon SDK instance to work with:

// Get CoreCon WP7 SDK

DatastoreManager dsmgrObj = new DatastoreManager(1033);

 

Platform WP7SDK = dsmgrObj.GetPlatforms().Single(p => p.Name == "New Windows Mobile 7 SDK");

 

Next up we’ll have to get a reference to either a WP7 physical device or a WP7 Emulator.
This demo will use the emulator, but if we set “useEmulator = false” this demo will try and connect to a physical WP7 device.

// Get Emulator / Device

bool useEmulator = true;

Device WP7Device = null;

if (useEmulator)

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Emulator");

else

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Device");

Now we’ll launch the WP7 Emulator/Device.
Note that the default WP7 Emulator Image is the one we’ll launch into, and in a previous blog post I’ve explained how to use the Unlocked ROM as the default ROM.

// Connect to WP7 Emulator / Device

Console.WriteLine("Connecting to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

WP7Device.Connect();

Console.WriteLine("Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device Connected...");

Next, we’ll have to check if our application is already installed, and if it is – we’ll uninstall it.
Since the the UpdateApplication Method in the current CoreCon API doesn’t work, this is our best bet on easily updating installed apps.

In order to Install or Uninstall our application, we’ll need it’s Application Product Identifier (GUID).
We can get the application GUID from the Properties/WMAppManifest.xml file.

 

We’ll write the code to check if an application is installed, and if it is – we’ll uninstall it.

Guid appID = new Guid("{5e75bba1-fbf6-463c-94ac-fa4a78f8fd12}");

RemoteApplication app;

if (WP7Device.IsApplicationInstalled(appID))

{

    Console.WriteLine("Uninstalling sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

    app = WP7Device.GetApplication(appID);

    app.Uninstall();

 

    Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP Uninstalled from Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

}

At this point, we’ll install our XAP.
In order to do that, we’ll need 3 pieces of information:
1. The location of our XAP.
2. The Application GUID.
3. The location of the application icon.

// Install XAP

Console.WriteLine("Installing sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

app = WP7Device.InstallApplication(

    appID,

    appID,

    "NormalApp",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\ApplicationIcon.png",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\Bin\Debug\WindowsPhoneApplication1.xap");

 

Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP installed to Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

The last step is to actually launch our application.

// Launch Application

Console.WriteLine("Launching sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

app.Launch();

Console.WriteLine("Launched sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

We’re done. And indeed when we run our sample application the app runs as expected:

 

So What is WP7 Automation good for?

There’s a lot of good use cases: Automating Unit tests, Loading Nightly builds into the emulator and even letting customers use the WP7 Emulator.
There’s really a plethora of reasons and situations WP7 Automation can prove useful in and it’s up to you to figure it out for your projects.

For instance in Vertigo, we’re using the WP7 Automation harness to run the WP7 Emulator on multi-touch laptops that our customers have.
So Vertigo’s customers, as part of an iterative process, get access to our current build without having to install or use Visual Studio 2010.

 

Access to Isolated Storage

One use-case in particular interests me, which is automating running all unit tests in the project after a Continuous Integration nightly build.

We can pretty much do all of the work to automate WP7 tests using WP7 Automation we’ve seen so far, but how do we get results into application? Or get instructions in?

The easiest method I can think off is communicate through cold storage – read & write files into Isolated Storage.

We’ll start off by writing a file into our WP7 Application IsoStore.
Remember that this code executes in the WP7 Emulator/Device.

public MainPage()

{

    InitializeComponent();

 

    SupportedOrientations = SupportedPageOrientation.Portrait | SupportedPageOrientation.Landscape;

 

    using (var isoStore = IsolatedStorageFile.GetUserStoreForApplication())

    using (var sw = new StreamWriter(isoStore.OpenFile("Foo.txt", FileMode.OpenOrCreate, FileAccess.Write)))

    {

        sw.Write("Hello WP7! (Written from WP7 IsoStore, read by Console Harness!)");

    }

}

Basically, We’ve written a Foo.txt file into our IsoStore and added some text into it.

Next, we would have used the RemoteIsolatedStorage class and get access to the emulator IsoStore, but that has not been enabled yet in CoreCon10.

We would have used RemoteApplication.GetIsolatedStorage() but that has not been implemented yet.

We’ll use a FileDeployer class instead.
There’s some reflection magic associated with getting a copy of a FileDeployer class that can be used for our application.

Thread.Sleep(10000);

//app.GetIsolatedStore(); <-- Throws NotImplementedException

object ConManServer = WP7Device.GetType().GetField("mConmanServer", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance).GetValue(WP7Device);

FileDeployer f = (FileDeployer)typeof(FileDeployer).GetConstructors(BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic)[0].Invoke(new object[] { ConManServer });

Next, we’ll copy the Foo.txt file from the application isolated storage into our local binary folder and read it into the console:

f.ReceiveFile(@"\Applications\Data\" + appID + @"\data\isolatedstore\Foo.txt", @"\Foo.txt");

 

Console.WriteLine("\t" + File.ReadAllText(@"foo.txt"));

 

When we run this sample we can see the text written from IsoStore showing up on our console.

And we’re done, we’ve esteblished a two-way communication channel between WP7 Emulator/Device and Managed .net code.  

 

Console WP7 Automation Harness Source Code

Here’s the source code we’ve built in this project:

// Get CoreCon WP7 SDK

DatastoreManager dsmgrObj = new DatastoreManager(1033);

 

Platform WP7SDK = dsmgrObj.GetPlatforms().Single(p => p.Name == "New Windows Mobile 7 SDK");

 

// Get Emulator / Device

bool useEmulator = true;

Device WP7Device = null;

if (useEmulator)

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Emulator");

else

    WP7Device = WP7SDK.GetDevices().Single(d => d.Name == "Windows Phone 7 Device");

 

// Connect to WP7 Emulator / Device

Console.WriteLine("Connecting to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

WP7Device.Connect();

Console.WriteLine("Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device Connected...");

 

 

Guid appID = new Guid("{5e75bba1-fbf6-463c-94ac-fa4a78f8fd12}");

RemoteApplication app;

if (WP7Device.IsApplicationInstalled(appID))

{

    Console.WriteLine("Uninstalling sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

    app = WP7Device.GetApplication(appID);

    app.Uninstall();

 

    Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP Uninstalled from Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

}

 

// Install XAP

Console.WriteLine("Installing sample XAP to Windows Phone 7 Emulator/Device...");

 

app = WP7Device.InstallApplication(

    appID,

    appID,

    "NormalApp",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\ApplicationIcon.png",

    @"D:\visual studio 2010\Projects\ConsoleApplication1\WindowsPhoneApplication1\Bin\Debug\WindowsPhoneApplication1.xap");

 

Console.WriteLine("Sample XAP installed to Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

// Launch Application

Console.WriteLine("Launching sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

app.Launch();

Console.WriteLine("Launched sample app on Windows Phone 7 Emulator...");

 

Console.WriteLine("Reading Foo.txt Isolated Storage file:");

 

Thread.Sleep(10000);

//app.GetIsolatedStore(); <-- Throws NotImplementedException

object ConManServer = WP7Device.GetType().GetField("mConmanServer", BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance).GetValue(WP7Device);

FileDeployer f = (FileDeployer)typeof(FileDeployer).GetConstructors(BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic)[0].Invoke(new object[] { ConManServer });

f.ReceiveFile(@"\Applications\Data\" + appID + @"\data\isolatedstore\Foo.txt", @"\Foo.txt");

 

Console.WriteLine("\t" + File.ReadAllText(@"foo.txt"));

 

Console.ReadLine();

 

Fin

In this blog post we’ve talked about why Automating the WP7 Emulator and Device deployment process is important and how to go about doing that.
Hopefully now you know how to automate WP7 XAP Deployment.

In the next blog post in this series we’ll talk about setting up a Continuous Integration build for WP7.

 

Leave a Comment

Are there any other use cases for WP7 Automation?
Are you planning on using this technique somewhere?
Was this a good blog post? Sound off in the comments.

 

Sincerely,

-- Justin Angel

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] #BehindThePrint 06: The Hidden Angle
items.content_html:
Behind the Scenes of Our Sandtable Creations

Through our Sandtable Exhibition projects, we explore the possibilities of 3D printing by creating detailed miniature worlds that bring together design, engineering, and craftsmanship.

In our #BehindThePrint series, we share the unexpected challenges, creative decisions, and practical lessons behind these creations.

Even the smallest architectural details in our miniature worlds can reveal unexpected 3D-printing challenges.

When the Corners Have Other Ideas

At first glance, there was nothing particularly unusual about the colorful geometric structures in our miniature climbing gym.

The raised details featured sloping edges designed at a 40° overhang angle. For our intended printing conditions, that seemed like a reasonable choice.

And for the most part, the prints looked fine.

Except for the corners.

While the straight edges appeared relatively clean, the corners developed rough, uneven surfaces. The problem was particularly noticeable around the green sections of the model.

The straight edges printed relatively cleanly, but the corners revealed unexpected surface defects

So what was different about those corners?

It looked like insufficient cooling was one factor affecting print quality. But the model’s geometry revealed another important part of the problem.

The corners weren’t actually following the same overhang angle as the edges.

And the difference was bigger than we might expect.

The Angle We Didn’t See

When designing an overhang, we usually pay attention to the angle of the sloping surface. If it falls within a range our printer can comfortably handle, the design should be reasonably printable.

Or so it seems.

The tricky part is that, on shapes with sharp corners, the angle we design along an edge isn’t necessarily the steepest angle the printer encounters.

Imagine a square column with a sloping section that gradually widens as it rises.

With every new layer, the edges extend slightly farther outward. Along a straight edge, this movement follows the intended 40° slope.

But something different happens at the corners.

Here, two edges meet, and their outward extensions combine diagonally. That means each corner reaches farther beyond the previous layer than the straight edges do.

Only a little farther, at first glance. But enough to change the effective overhang angle significantly.

The corner extends farther outward than the straight edge, creating a steeper effective overhang between successive layers.

For our four-sided shape, the numbers reveal just how much this matters.

The straight edges were designed at 40°.

At the corners, however, the effective overhang angle reached approximately 49.9°.

That’s almost 10° steeper than the original design angle!

For this production case, we were working with a maximum overhang target of 45°, allowing a margin for less favorable printing conditions.

The straight edges were within that target. The corners had quietly crossed it.

Suddenly, those rough corners made much more sense.

What Happens When We Change the Shape?

The interesting thing about this problem is that we don’t necessarily need to change the printer settings to address it.

Sometimes, we can make geometry work in our favor. And there are several ways to approach it.

More Sides, Less Trouble

What if our square shape wasn’t quite so square?

Imagine replacing the four-sided prism with one that has eight sides. The top-down shape becomes a little closer to a circle, and its corners become less pronounced.

That also changes how far those corners extend beyond the previous layer.

With the same 40° edge angle, the calculated maximum corner angle drops from approximately 49.9° to just 42.2°.

Adding more sides brings the effective corner overhang closer to the intended 40° edge angle.

The columns with multiple sides never faced the printing issues like the 4 sided version did

Of course, adding sides changes the appearance of the model. If a sharp, square shape is essential to the design, this might not be the ideal solution.

Fortunately, it isn’t the only option.

A Gentler Slope

Another approach is to keep the four-sided shape but reduce its straight edge angle.

For example, changing the edge angle from 40° to 35° reduces the calculated corner angle to approximately 44.7°.

That brings even the corners within our 45° design target.

It’s a relatively straightforward geometric adjustment, although the gentler slope also changes the proportions of the feature.

A gentler slope reduces the effective overhang angle at the corners without changing the number of sides.

Or Simply Soften the Corners

There’s also a third possibility: rounding the corners themselves.

Instead of allowing two straight edges to meet at a sharp point, we can introduce a curved transition.

This reduces the pronounced diagonal extension at the corner and can bring the maximum overhang closer to the intended edge angle.

Rounded corners reduce the abrupt change in geometry responsible for the steeper corner overhang.

Which approach makes the most sense depends on the design.

Sometimes we can change the overall shape. Other times, preserving its appearance matters more.

The important thing is understanding what the geometry is doing before deciding how to improve it.

By this point, you probably wonder about all these nice diagrams and calculations shared above. We have this handy little tool as a download link for you.

Feel free to check it out and explore how the straight slope or corner count will affect the corner angle.

A Different Way to Look at Overhangs

Our miniature climbing-gym component highlights a detail that’s surprisingly easy to overlook.

When we check an overhang, we’re often looking at the most obvious sloping surface. But the printer doesn’t only have to deal with that surface. It also has to build the corners where those surfaces meet.

And as we’ve seen, those corners can behave quite differently.

This doesn’t mean every sharp corner will cause printing problems. Actual print quality also depends on cooling, material, speed, and other conditions.

But it does give us another useful consideration when designing parts with overhangs: check the most demanding part of the geometry, not just the angle that’s easiest to see.

Sometimes, the trickiest overhang isn’t on the surface we’re looking at. It’s hiding right around the corner.

More Stories Behind the Print

From unexpected layer lines to hidden geometric challenges, our Sandtable projects keep reminding us that small design details can make a big difference.

Have you ever encountered a print that looked perfectly reasonable in the model but turned out differently than expected?

We’d love to hear what you discovered.

See you in the next #BehindThePrint!

items.content_html: IKEA has listed the Liljebagge radiator thermostat for €14.99 in its German online store, but it cannot be ordered there yet. According to HomeKits, sales are scheduled to begin in January 2027. Sales could begin earlier at some individual stores. The device is designed for water-based radiators and communicates via Matter over Thread. Integration requires a Thread border router, but not necessarily the IKEA Dirigera hub; the temperature can also be set directly on the thermostat. However, initial customer reviews from Sweden mention discrepancies in temperature readings and bothersome noises during adjustment.

items.title: [smarthomeassistent.de] Nginx vulnerabilities threaten smart home systems; Frigate releases emergency update
items.content_html: The developers of the open-source network video recorder Frigate released version 0.18.3 on November 19, which fixes a critical vulnerability in the bundled nginx web server. nginx 1.27.4 was affected: with HTTP/2 enabled, attackers could execute code without authentication via an accessible Frigate web server. Frigate’s developers describe the flaw as a vulnerability that allows code execution with root privileges; according to security researchers, however, escalating from the nginx process to root privileges on the host also requires a Linux kernel vulnerability. The vulnerability is one of ten security flaws that manufacturer F5 fixed with an nginx update released on November 18. F5 rates five of them 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. According to security researchers, two HTTP/2 flaws allow remote attacks without authentication. Frigate 0.18.3 updates nginx to version 1.30.7 and also restricts certain options in the go2rtc camera-streaming component. The update is particularly urgent for operators who have made Frigate’s web interface accessible over the internet; the security advisories list ports 5000 and 8971. Installations accessible only on the home network should also be updated, as a compromised device could serve as an entry point. Frigate recommends backing up the configuration and database before updating. For standalone nginx installations, the security advisories list version 1.30.7 for the stable branch and 1.31.9 for the mainline branch as the fixed releases.

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] AI Model Pictures Have to GO!
items.content_html:
This notification, just dropped - are Makerworld listening???

MakerWorld Community Guidelines Update

2026-11-19 03:58

Hi MakerWorld Community,

We are updating the rules for model images, focusing on improving their authenticity and consistency with the actual models, in order to continuously enhance the quality of content and the user experience within the community.

This update includes three core changes:

  1. The cover image must show the complete model, match the model files, and accurately reflect the finished 3D print.
  2. The cover image must match the structure, material appearance, and color regions shown in real printed images .
  3. When uploading a model, you must provide at least three photos of the actual 3D print from different angles, in addition to the cover image. These photos must match the model files.

We are also reminding you to follow the existing image rules for Print Profiles.

Detailed rules, examples, execution specifics, and important considerations have been provided in the community announcement.

Click here to view the full announcement

Thank you for your understanding and cooperation as we work together to create a more trustworthy creative environment.

MakerWorld Team

items.content_html: Three new or expanded integrations provide additional sensor data for Home Assistant: the community integration HomePod Sensor Link reads temperature and humidity directly from Apple speakers, an update to the X-Sense SBS50 base station expands the integration of compatible security devices, and a new community project integrates EnOcean multisensors via Bluetooth. HomePod Sensor Link has been available in the Home Assistant marketplace since November 16. However, setup requires exported HomeKit keys and changes to macOS security features. X-Sense is rolling out firmware 1.8.7 gradually; after the update, the connection can be configured in the app. The EnOcean integration supports temperature, brightness, motion, and vibration, among other features.

items.title: [smarthomeassistent.de] Tests reveal differences in smart radiator thermostats and ongoing costs
items.content_html: Comparative tests of smart radiator thermostats reveal significant differences in operation, system requirements, and additional costs. In IMTEST’s comparison of ten devices priced between 30 and 100 euros, the Homematic IP Evo radiator thermostat came out on top; according to IMTEST, it also offers geo-fencing and hydraulic balancing without a subscription. The least expensive model tested, the TP-Link Kasa KE100, costs 29.90 euros per thermostat but showed weaknesses in window detection and geo-fencing. In another comparison, the Aqara W600 and the Bosch Radiator Thermostat 2 [+M] each received a score of 1.4; both require a hub. The Shelly TRV, which connects directly to Wi-Fi, received a score of 2.6. Compatibility depends, among other things, on the valve connection and the hub already in place; some features incur subscription fees.

items.title: [Jan Bilek] Grond spins – development update, 15 November 2026
items.content_html: This article continues the Grond project by developing its traction system. After refining an initial concept with ChatGPT/Codex and modeling it in OpenSCAD, the author sourced components and assembled the mechanism with Serge at his DaVinci workshop. A video demonstrates the working system and control testing. Next: the first 500mm test tube.

items.title: [homekitnews.com] Aqara launches six Matter lights with Thread and Zigbee
items.content_html: Smart-home provider Aqara has launched six new lights for indoor and outdoor use. The range includes a floor lamp, an LED strip, a recessed spotlight, E14 bulbs, a string light, and permanently installed outdoor lights. All models support Thread and Zigbee; via Thread, they can be integrated into compatible smart-home systems using Matter. The devices have been available since November 17. Aqara lists prices starting at 20.99 euros in its EU store; a 20 percent introductory discount with the code AQARALIGHT11 ends on November 18. To use Matter over Thread, users need a compatible controller and a Thread border router. Aqara-specific extra features, on the other hand, require a compatible Aqara hub.
